title: Lotus leaf: self-cleaning, water-repellent surface
summary: The lotus leaf stays clean without detergent: its surface is covered in tiny bumps topped with wax crystals, so water beads up and rolls off, picking up dirt particles on the way. This 'lotus effect' is the model for self-cleaning paints, facade coatings and water-repellent textiles.
structure: micrometre-scale papillae covered with nanoscale epicuticular wax crystals
mechanism: the rough, waxy surface keeps the water contact angle very high, so droplets roll rather than slide and carry loose particles away

performance.metric: static water contact angle, lower bound (superhydrophobic range)

evidence.citation: Barthlott W, Neinhuis C (1997). Purity of the sacred lotus, or escape from contamination in biological surfaces. Planta 202: 1-8.
Neinhuis C, Barthlott W (1997). Characterization and distribution of water-repellent, self-cleaning plant surfaces. Annals of Botany 79: 667-677.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The effect needs rain or rinsing water and is lost when the micro-structure is worn, scratched or covered by oily dirt; durability outdoors is the usual weak point.

title: Gecko toe hairs that clean themselves while walking
summary: Gecko feet pick up dust but lose it again after a few steps on a clean surface, because particles stick more strongly to the surface than to the very fine toe hairs. It is a dry self-cleaning route for reusable adhesives and grippers that would otherwise clog with dirt.
structure: branched keratin hairs ending in nanoscale spatulae
mechanism: a dirt particle touches far fewer spatulae than it touches the substrate, so it adheres more to the substrate and is shed during repeated steps

evidence.citation: Hansen WR, Autumn K (2005). Evidence for self-cleaning in gecko setae. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 102: 385-389.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Shown for particles on clean glass in the lab; behaviour with oily or wet dirt is different, and synthetic copies self-clean less well than the animal.

title: Pitcher plant rim: slippery liquid-coated surface
summary: The rim of some pitcher plants becomes extremely slippery when wet: a film of water held in its micro-ridges makes insects aquaplane into the trap. Engineers copied the idea as lubricant-infused surfaces that shed water, oil, ice and dirt, and repair themselves when scratched because the liquid flows back.
structure: radial micro-ridges that hold a continuous liquid film
mechanism: a stable liquid layer locked into the surface texture leaves nothing solid for drops, insects or dirt to grip

evidence.citation: Bohn HF, Federle W (2004). Insect aquaplaning: Nepenthes pitcher plants capture prey with the peristome, a fully wettable water-lubricated anisotropic surface. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 101: 14138-14143.
Wong TS, Kang SH, Tang SKY, Smythe EJ, Hatton BD, Grinthal A, Aizenberg J (2011). Bioinspired self-repairing slippery surfaces with pressure-stable omniphobicity. Nature 477: 443-447.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Engineered versions depend on keeping the lubricant in place; it can drain, evaporate or wash out, and the lubricant itself must be safe for the use.

title: Cicada wing: dew drops that jump off and take dirt with them
summary: On some cicada wings, condensing dew drops merge and suddenly jump off the surface, carrying dust with them. This gives a self-cleaning route that needs no rain or rinsing, of interest for condensers, solar panels and building surfaces in humid places.
structure: dense arrays of nanoscale cones with a water-repellent coating
mechanism: when small condensed drops coalesce, the released surface energy launches the merged drop away from the water-repellent surface, taking particles along

evidence.citation: Wisdom KM, Watson JA, Qu X, Liu F, Watson GS, Chen CH (2013). Self-cleaning of superhydrophobic surfaces by self-propelled jumping condensate. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 110: 7992-7997.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Works only under condensing conditions and on intact nanostructures; field durability of synthetic versions is not established.

title: Insect wing nanopillars that kill bacteria on contact
summary: The wings of some cicadas carry dense nanopillars that stretch and rupture certain bacterial cells that settle on them, without any chemical biocide. The idea is studied for hygienic surfaces in food processing, medical devices and water systems.
structure: regular arrays of nanopillars roughly a hundred nanometres apart
mechanism: cells that adhere across several pillars are stretched between them until the cell envelope fails

evidence.citation: Ivanova EP, Hasan J, Webb HK, et al. (2012). Natural bactericidal surfaces: mechanical rupture of Pseudomonas aeruginosa cells by cicada wings. Small 8: 2489-2494.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Effect differs strongly between bacterial species (several tougher bacteria survived in later work), and dead cells can build up and cover the pillars.

title: Rice leaf and butterfly wing: directional water and dirt shedding
summary: Rice leaves and butterfly wings combine water-repellent texture with grooves aligned in one direction, so drops roll off along a preferred path and take dirt with them. Lab copies combine low drag with self-cleaning for pipes, boat hulls and coatings.
structure: parallel micro-grooves with hierarchical wax papillae
mechanism: anisotropic texture lets drops roll easily along the grooves but not across them, steering run-off and dirt removal

evidence.citation: Bixler GD, Bhushan B (2012). Bioinspired rice leaf and butterfly wing surface structures combining shark skin and lotus effects. Soft Matter 8: 11271-11284.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Results are from lab-made replicas in flow cells; scale-up and wear resistance are open questions.

title: Springtail skin: repels water and oils with mushroom-shaped texture
summary: Springtails, tiny soil animals, breathe through skin that stays dry even under water and resists oily liquids. Their skin texture has overhanging, mushroom-shaped edges that pin liquids on top, an approach for coatings that repel oils and stay clean without fluorinated chemistry.
structure: nanoscale comb-like network with overhanging (re-entrant) edges
mechanism: overhanging edges hold the liquid surface up so that even low-surface-tension liquids do not penetrate the texture

evidence.citation: Hensel R, Helbig R, Aland S, Braun HG, Voigt A, Neinhuis C, Werner C (2013). Wetting resistance at its topographical limit: the benefit of mushroom and serif T structures. Langmuir 29: 1100-1112.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Mechanism derived from lab replicas; overhanging textures are hard to manufacture at scale and easily damaged.

title: Floating fern Salvinia: keeps a stable air layer under water
summary: Leaves of the floating fern Salvinia hold a layer of air when submerged for long periods. Water-repellent egg-beater-shaped hairs carry small water-attracting tips that pin the water surface. Copying this could cut friction on ship hulls and keep surfaces from fouling.
structure: egg-beater-shaped water-repellent hairs with water-attracting tips
mechanism: hydrophilic tips pin the air-water interface, so the trapped air layer survives pressure changes and turbulence longer

evidence.citation: Barthlott W, Schimmel T, Wiersch S, et al. (2010). The Salvinia paradox: superhydrophobic surfaces with hydrophilic pins for air retention under water. Advanced Materials 22: 2325-2328.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Ship-hull drag savings have been projected, not demonstrated at full scale.

title: Shark skin denticles: drag and swimsuits
summary: Shark skin is covered in small tooth-like scales (denticles) with ridges. Studies on flexible skin samples show the denticles can change the flow near the skin and improve swimming performance. Riblet films for aircraft and pipes draw on the same idea.
structure: overlapping ridged dermal denticles
mechanism: ridged denticles alter near-wall flow (vortex formation and the boundary layer), which can raise thrust and reduce drag on a flexing body

evidence.citation: Oeffner J, Lauder GV (2012). The hydrodynamic function of shark skin and two biomimetic applications. Journal of Experimental Biology 215: 785-795.
Dean B, Bhushan B (2010). Shark-skin surfaces for fluid-drag reduction in turbulent flow: a review. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 368: 4775-4806.

popular_claim_note: Swimsuits sold as 'shark skin' (for example Speedo's Fastskin fabric) are often cited as proof. Oeffner & Lauder (2012) tested the fabric and found its surface texture gave no swimming benefit; any advantage of those suits has to come from other properties, not from copying denticles.
caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Benefits measured on lab foils; engineered riblets give small drag savings only in a narrow flow range and lose them when fouled.

title: Shark-skin texture that discourages fouling without biocides
summary: A micro-pattern of ridged diamonds inspired by shark skin makes it harder for algae spores and bacteria to settle. It is used on surfaces where biocide coatings are unwanted, such as hospital touch surfaces, and studied for hulls and water infrastructure.
structure: engineered diamond pattern of parallel micro-ridges of different lengths
mechanism: feature size and spacing below the size of settling cells reduce the stable attachment points they can find

evidence.citation: Schumacher JF, Carman ML, Estes TG, Feinberg AW, Wilson LH, Callow ME, Callow JA, Finlay JA, Brennan AB (2007). Engineered antifouling microtopographies - effect of feature size, geometry, and roughness on settlement of zoospores of the green alga Ulva. Biofouling 23: 55-62.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The pattern is inspired by, not copied from, shark skin; lab settlement tests with one alga do not predict all fouling organisms in the field.

title: Namib desert beetle: capturing water from fog
summary: Some Namib desert beetles drink fog: they face the wind and let fog droplets gather on their bumpy back until the drops are big enough to run down to the mouth. Their mix of water-attracting bumps and water-repellent background inspired fog-harvesting surfaces and nets that capture water from air.
structure: smooth bumps that attract water on a waxy, water-repellent background
mechanism: drops nucleate and grow on the bumps, then roll off along the water-repellent areas towards the mouth

evidence.citation: Parker AR, Lawrence CR (2001). Water capture by a desert beetle. Nature 414: 33-34.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Water yields per beetle are tiny, and how much the surface pattern matters compared with posture and fog conditions is still discussed; engineered fog collectors need frequent fog to be worthwhile.

title: Spider silk knots that collect water droplets from air
summary: When the capture silk of some spiders dries after fog, it forms periodic knots joined by thin stretches. Water droplets move along the thread towards the knots and grow there, a pattern copied in fibres that capture and move water from humid air.
structure: spindle-shaped knots of random nanofibrils joined by aligned-fibril joints
mechanism: differences in surface energy and in curvature between knots and joints push droplets towards the knots

evidence.citation: Zheng Y, Bai H, Huang Z, Tian X, Nie FQ, Zhao Y, Zhai J, Jiang L (2010). Directional water collection on wetted spider silk. Nature 463: 640-643.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Describes the thread's shape and texture only, not silk chemistry; artificial fibres collect small volumes in lab fog chambers.

title: Cactus spines that capture and move fog water
summary: Cactus spines from a fog-exposed species catch fog droplets at their tips and move them towards the base without any pumping, helped by the conical shape and graded micro-grooves. The design informs fog collectors and passive liquid transport.
structure: conical spines with barbs at the tip and grooves graded along their length
mechanism: the cone shape creates a pressure difference (Laplace pressure) and the graded grooves a wettability gradient, both driving drops from tip to base

evidence.citation: Ju J, Bai H, Zheng Y, Zhao T, Fang R, Jiang L (2012). A multi-structural and multi-functional integrated fog collection system in cactus. Nature Communications 3: 1247.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Measured on single spines in a lab fog stream.

title: Namib dune grass that waters itself with fog
summary: A grass endemic to the Namib dunes catches fog on its grooved leaves and channels the water down to its roots. It is a living example of passive fog capture and drainage to a point of use, relevant to fog harvesting and landscape water design.
structure: longitudinal grooves along upright leaves
mechanism: fog drops gather on the leaves and run down the grooves to the plant base

evidence.citation: Roth-Nebelsick A, Ebner M, Miranda T, et al. (2012). Leaf surface structures enable the endemic Namib desert grass Stipagrostis sabulicola to irrigate itself with fog water. Journal of the Royal Society Interface 9: 1965-1974.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Field observations in one desert; transferring the geometry to collectors has not been field-tested at scale.

title: Texas horned lizard skin: channels that move water in one direction
summary: The Texas horned lizard can collect water on its back and move it through capillary channels between its scales towards the mouth. The channel geometry makes water flow preferentially one way, a 'liquid diode' idea for passive cooling-lubricant and water transport.
structure: interconnected capillary channels that narrow and widen periodically
mechanism: asymmetric widening of the channels stops the water front in one direction while letting it advance in the other

evidence.citation: Comanns P, Buchberger G, Buchsbaum A, et al. (2015). Directional, passive liquid transport: the Texas horned lizard as a model for a biomimetic 'liquid diode'. Journal of the Royal Society Interface 12: 20150415.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Lab replicas only; the authors also explored lubricant transport for machining, which is a proposal rather than an industrial practice.

title: Gecko feet: strong, reusable dry adhesion
summary: Geckos climb smooth walls with millions of tiny hairs on their toes that stick through weak molecular forces, no glue involved. The grip turns on and off with the angle of the toe, so it can be reused many times. It inspired dry, residue-free adhesives and robot grippers.
structure: hierarchy of setae branching into hundreds of nanoscale spatulae
mechanism: very close contact of many tiny spatulae adds up van der Waals forces; changing the pull angle peels them off easily

evidence.citation: Autumn K, Liang YA, Hsieh ST, Zesch W, Chan WP, Kenny TW, Fearing R, Full RJ (2000). Adhesive force of a single gecko foot-hair. Nature 405: 681-685.
Autumn K, Sitti M, Liang YA, et al. (2002). Evidence for van der Waals adhesion in gecko setae. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 99: 12252-12256.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Synthetic gecko adhesives work best on smooth, clean surfaces and lose grip with dust and wear; they do not match the animal's durability.

title: Mussel glue that sticks under water
summary: Mussels anchor to wet rocks with threads tipped by adhesive proteins rich in the amino acid DOPA. Copying that chemistry gave coatings and glues that bond in wet conditions. Because the trait is biochemical, the record waits for legal review before it can be served.
structure: protein-based adhesive plaque at the end of each byssus thread
mechanism: catechol (DOPA) side groups bind to wet mineral and metal surfaces and cross-link the glue

evidence.citation: Waite JH, Tanzer ML (1981). Polyphenolic substance of Mytilus edulis: novel adhesive containing L-dopa and hydroxyproline. Science 212: 1038-1040.
Lee H, Dellatore SM, Miller WM, Messersmith PB (2007). Mussel-inspired surface chemistry for multifunctional coatings. Science 318: 426-430.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Quarantined: biochemical trait, legal review pending (Nagoya / EU 511/2014 reading to confirm). Not served until cleared.

title: Spider dragline silk: tough fibre spun at room temperature
summary: Spiders spin dragline silk, a protein fibre that is both strong and stretchy, from a water-based solution at room temperature by controlling flow, acidity and ion content in the spinning duct. Engineers study it for low-energy fibre production. Because the trait is biochemical, the record waits for legal review before it can be served.
trait: dragline silk and its spinning duct
structure: silk proteins stored as a liquid crystal and drawn through a tapering duct
mechanism: controlled shear, water removal and changes in pH and ions in the duct make the proteins line up and solidify into a fibre

evidence.citation: Vollrath F, Knight DP (2001). Liquid crystalline spinning of spider silk. Nature 410: 541-548.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Quarantined: biochemical trait, legal review pending. Recombinant silk fibres have so far not matched natural dragline properties at scale.

title: Burdock burrs: hook-and-loop fastening
summary: Burdock seed heads carry many small hooks that catch on animal fur and clothing. This observation led to the hook-and-loop fastener, which joins and separates parts many times without screws or glue and makes products easier to take apart.
structure: stiff bracts ending in small flexible hooks
mechanism: many small hooks engage loops or fibres; each hook releases when bent, so the joint opens without damage and can be reused

evidence.citation: de Mestral G (1955). Velvet type fabric and method of producing same. US Patent 2,717,437.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The burr-to-fastener story comes from the inventor's own account and patent; the patent text describes the fabric, not burdock biology.

title: Nacre (mother-of-pearl): brick-and-mortar toughness
summary: Nacre, the inner layer of many shells, is made almost entirely of brittle chalk-like mineral yet is far tougher than the mineral alone. Thin mineral tablets are stacked like bricks with a little soft organic 'mortar' between them, so cracks are deflected and energy is absorbed. It inspires tough ceramics, composites and impact-resistant panels.
structure: aragonite tablets about half a micrometre thick layered with thin organic sheets
mechanism: tablet sliding, crack deflection and bridging at the soft interfaces spread damage instead of letting one crack run through

evidence.citation: Jackson AP, Vincent JFV, Turner RM (1988). The mechanical design of nacre. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 234: 415-440.
Munch E, Launey ME, Alsem DH, Saiz E, Tomsia AP, Ritchie RO (2008). Tough, bio-inspired hybrid materials. Science 322: 1516-1520.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Nacre-like synthetic materials are mostly lab-scale; the organic interlayer chemistry of the shell is not part of this record.

title: Trabecular bone: light lattices that follow the loads
summary: The spongy bone inside our joints is a lattice of struts and plates that lines up with the loads it carries and is rebuilt when loads change. It is a model for lightweight lattice parts, for example 3D-printed metal brackets for cars and aircraft that put material only where stress needs it.
structure: open lattice of trabeculae aligned with principal stress directions
mechanism: bone cells add material where strain is high and remove it where it is low, so the lattice converges on a light, load-matched structure

evidence.citation: Huiskes R, Ruimerman R, van Lenthe GH, Janssen JD (2000). Effects of mechanical forces on maintenance and adaptation of form in trabecular bone. Nature 405: 704-706.
Gibson LJ (2005). Biomechanics of cellular solids. Journal of Biomechanics 38: 377-399.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The engineering analogue is topology optimisation and lattice design; bone also repairs itself, which printed metal parts cannot.

title: Tree growth rules for lighter, fatigue-resistant parts
summary: Trees add wood where stresses peak, for example around branch joints, until stress is spread evenly over the surface. Simulating this growth rule in software removes stress peaks from machine parts, giving lighter components that resist fatigue cracking, an approach used for car and machine parts.
structure: thickened wood at notches, forks and branch junctions
mechanism: growth is faster where surface stress is higher, which flattens stress peaks (the axiom of uniform stress)

evidence.citation: Mattheck C, Burkhardt S (1990). A new method of structural shape optimization based on biological growth. International Journal of Fatigue 12: 185-190.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The software method is an engineering abstraction of tree growth, not a model of wood biology.

title: Bamboo: fibres graded for a light, stiff stem
summary: Bamboo stems are hollow tubes in which strong fibres are packed densely towards the outside and sparsely inside. This grading gives high bending stiffness for little weight, a pattern used in thinking about lightweight tubes, car parts and graded composites.
structure: vascular fibre bundles whose density increases from inner to outer wall
mechanism: putting the stiffest material furthest from the bending axis maximises bending stiffness per unit mass

evidence.citation: Amada S, Ichikawa Y, Munekata T, Nagase Y, Shimizu H (1997). Fiber texture and mechanical graded structure of bamboo. Composites Part B 28: 13-20.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Bamboo as a building material varies widely between species and harvests; this record covers the grading principle.

title: Glass sponge skeleton: light, damage-tolerant lattice
summary: The deep-sea Venus' flower basket builds a cylindrical lattice of glass with diagonal bracing and layered glass struts. It is very stiff for its weight and tolerates damage, a model for lightweight lattice towers, tubes and structural parts.
structure: square-grid glass lattice with diagonal bracing; struts made of laminated silica
mechanism: bracing resists shear and buckling while thin organic layers between silica laminae stop cracks

evidence.citation: Aizenberg J, Weaver JC, Thanawala MS, Sundar VC, Morse DE, Fratzl P (2005). Skeleton of Euplectella sp.: structural hierarchy from the nanoscale to the macroscale. Science 309: 275-278.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Structural analyses of copied lattices are mostly computational or small-scale.

title: Diatom shells: strong, light micro-lattices
summary: Diatoms, single-celled algae, build glass shells patterned with ribs and pores that are remarkably strong for their weight and protect the cell from being crushed. The rib and honeycomb patterns are studied as templates for lightweight panels and structural parts.
structure: ribbed and perforated silica shells with honeycomb-like chambers
mechanism: ribs and chambered layers spread loads so the thin shell resists crushing

evidence.citation: Hamm CE, Merkel R, Springer O, Jurkojc P, Maier C, Prechtel K, Smetacek V (2003). Architecture and material properties of diatom shells provide effective mechanical protection. Nature 421: 841-843.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Shell strength measured on microscopic cells; translation to engineering scale relies on design analogy, not direct scaling.

title: Mantis shrimp club: impact-resistant, crack-stopping composite
summary: The peacock mantis shrimp smashes shells with a club that survives thousands of high-speed blows. Its fibres are laid in a helical (twisted plywood) pattern that forces cracks to twist and stop. This inspires impact-resistant composites for car parts, helmets and protective panels.
structure: mineralised impact surface over a helicoidal (twisted plywood) fibre region
mechanism: helically stacked fibre layers make cracks follow a twisting path, absorbing energy and preventing catastrophic failure

evidence.citation: Weaver JC, Milliron GW, Miserez A, et al. (2012). The stomatopod dactyl club: a formidable damage-tolerant biological hammer. Science 336: 1275-1280.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Helicoidal composites have been made in labs; impact gains depend strongly on layup and matrix.

title: Boxfish body shape and the 'bionic car'
summary: The boxfish has a stiff, boxy body made of bony plates. Carmakers presented it as a model for a roomy, low-drag and self-stabilising car body. Later fluid studies found the shape actually makes the fish less stable, helping it manoeuvre.
structure: rigid, box-shaped body armour of fused bony plates
mechanism: the flow around the boxy carapace produces forces that turn the body away from its course, i.e. destabilising rather than self-correcting

evidence.citation: Van Wassenbergh S, van Manen K, Marcroft TA, Alfaro ME, Stamhuis EJ (2015). Boxfish swimming paradox resolved: forces by the flow of water around the body promote manoeuvrability. Journal of the Royal Society Interface 12: 20141146.

popular_claim_note: Mercedes-Benz's 2005 'Bionic' concept car was presented as copying the boxfish for low drag and self-stability. Van Wassenbergh et al. (2015) found the shape destabilises the fish (good for manoeuvring), so the stability part of the story does not hold.
caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Car drag figures from the concept were company claims, not independent tests.

title: Humpback whale flipper bumps: delayed stall for blades and fans
summary: Humpback whales have rounded bumps (tubercles) along the front edge of their flippers. In wind-tunnel tests these bumps let a flipper model reach steeper angles before stalling, which is studied for wind turbine blades, fans and pumps.
structure: rounded tubercles along the leading edge
mechanism: tubercles create streamwise vortices that keep flow attached behind them, softening and delaying stall

performance.metric: increase in stall angle of a scale flipper model with tubercles

evidence.citation: Fish FE, Battle JM (1995). Hydrodynamic design of the humpback whale flipper. Journal of Morphology 225: 51-60.
Miklosovic DS, Murray MM, Howle LE, Fish FE (2004). Leading-edge tubercles delay stall on humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) flippers. Physics of Fluids 16: L39-L42.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Gains depend on speed and blade design; at some conditions tubercles reduce maximum lift. Commercial benefit claims for fans are not independently verified here.

title: Owl feathers: quiet flight for fans and turbines
summary: Owls fly almost silently thanks to comb-like serrations on the leading edge of the wing, fringes on the trailing edge and a soft, velvety feather surface. Copying these features reduces noise from fans, wind turbines and ventilation systems.
structure: leading-edge serrations, trailing-edge fringes and a porous velvety surface
mechanism: the features break up and soften the pressure fluctuations at wing edges that create aerodynamic noise

evidence.citation: Jaworski JW, Peake N (2020). Aeroacoustics of silent owl flight. Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics 52: 395-420.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Noise reductions vary with frequency and design; which owl feature matters most is still debated.

title: Kingfisher beak and the Shinkansen bullet-train nose
summary: Kingfishers dive into water with little splash. The nose of Japan's 500 series Shinkansen is widely said to copy the kingfisher beak to reduce the boom when trains exit tunnels. Diving kingfishers do show drag-reducing head shapes, but the train's energy and speed figures have not been independently tested.
structure: long, tapering beak blending into the head
mechanism: a gradually increasing cross-section reduces the sudden pressure change when entering a denser medium

evidence.citation: Crandell KE, Howe RO, Falkingham PL (2019). Repeated evolution of drag reduction at the air-water interface in diving kingfishers. Journal of the Royal Society Interface 16: 20190125.

popular_claim_note: The widely repeated figures (about 15% less energy, 10% faster, quieter tunnel exits) trace back to talks and articles by the train's engineer, not to an independent study. The kingfisher paper cited here concerns the birds, not the train.
caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Tunnel-boom reduction by long tapered noses is standard rail engineering; the role of the kingfisher was inspiration, not a measured transfer.

title: Countercurrent heat exchange in animal limbs
summary: Whales, wading birds and many other animals keep heat in their core by running warm outgoing blood vessels right next to cold returning ones, so heat passes across before it reaches the extremities. Industrial counterflow heat exchangers use the same principle to recover waste heat.
trait: blood vessel arrangement in fins, flippers and legs
structure: arteries surrounded by or paired with returning veins (rete arrangements)
mechanism: flows in opposite directions keep a temperature difference along the whole contact length, so most heat is transferred back before it is lost

evidence.citation: Scholander PF, Schevill WE (1955). Counter-current vascular heat exchange in the fins of whales. Journal of Applied Physiology 8: 279-282.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Counterflow heat exchangers are mature engineering; the biological example illustrates the principle rather than adding a new design.

title: Branching networks that minimise pumping energy (Murray's law)
summary: Blood vessels and plant veins branch so that the energy needed to pump fluid and to maintain the network is as low as possible, following a simple rule on how branch diameters relate. Engineers use the rule to size pipe, cooling and distribution networks.
structure: branching vessels whose radii follow a cube law at each junction
mechanism: balancing friction losses against the cost of the fluid volume gives an optimum where the cube of the parent radius equals the sum of the cubes of the daughters

evidence.citation: Murray CD (1926). The physiological principle of minimum work: I. The vascular system and the cost of blood volume. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 12: 207-214.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The rule assumes laminar flow and a specific cost function; turbulent pipe networks need different scaling.

title: Slime mould: growing efficient, resilient transport networks
summary: The slime mould Physarum, given food sources placed like cities around Tokyo, grew a network of tubes similar to the real rail network in efficiency and resilience. Simple local rules (reinforce busy tubes, let idle ones fade) can be used to design distribution networks for water, energy and logistics.
structure: network of protoplasmic tubes linking food sources
mechanism: tubes carrying more flow thicken and the rest shrink, trading total length against efficiency and fault tolerance

evidence.citation: Tero A, Takagi S, Saigusa T, Ito K, Bebber DP, Fricker MD, Yumiki K, Kobayashi R, Nakagaki T (2010). Rules for biologically inspired adaptive network design. Science 327: 439-442.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. An algorithmic inspiration; it does not replace engineering network optimisation with real costs and constraints.

title: Termite mound ventilation and the Eastgate building
summary: Large termite mounds exchange gases between the nest and outside air. Recent work shows the mound walls and conduits use daily temperature swings and wind to drive air movement, more like a lung than a chimney. Designers use the idea for passive ventilation and cooling in buildings, but the popular story behind it is wrong.
structure: porous walls with a network of surface conduits and a central chimney
mechanism: daily heating and cooling of the mound surface, plus wind, set up shifting air flows that ventilate the nest

evidence.citation: Turner JS, Soar RC (2008). Beyond biomimicry: what termites can tell us about realizing the living building. Proceedings of the First International Conference on Industrialized, Intelligent Construction (I3CON), Loughborough University.
King H, Ocko S, Mahadevan L (2015). Termite mounds harness diurnal temperature oscillations for ventilation. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 112: 11589-11593.

popular_claim_note: The Eastgate Centre in Harare is often described as cooled 'like a termite mound'. Turner & Soar (2008) showed that the model of mound ventilation behind that story (a steady chimney that holds the nest at a constant temperature) is mistaken; Eastgate's cooling is a conventional night-flushed thermal-mass design, and its energy savings say nothing about termites.
caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The two studies looked at different termite species and climates; mound ventilation is still being researched.

title: Saharan silver ant: hairs that reflect sunlight and shed heat
summary: Saharan silver ants forage in extreme heat. Their triangular hairs reflect visible and near-infrared sunlight and help radiate heat in the mid-infrared, keeping the body cooler. The idea feeds into passive cooling coatings and textiles that reduce cooling energy for buildings and vehicles.
structure: hairs with a triangular cross-section and corrugated surfaces
mechanism: total internal reflection and scattering in the hairs reflect sunlight while the hair layer emits strongly in the infrared window

evidence.citation: Shi NN, Tsai CC, Camino F, Bernard GD, Yu N, Wehner R (2015). Keeping cool: Enhanced optical reflection and radiative heat dissipation in Saharan silver ants. Science 349: 298-301.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Temperature benefit measured on ants; building-scale radiative cooling products are engineered separately and depend on climate.

title: White beetle scales: brilliant white without pigment
summary: Cyphochilus beetles are bright white because their thin scales contain a disordered network of fibres that scatters all colours of light very efficiently. This is a route to white paints, cosmetics and reflective coatings that need less or no titanium dioxide, and to sunlight-reflecting surfaces that keep buildings cooler.
structure: random network of chitin filaments inside scales a few micrometres thick
mechanism: the disordered filament network scatters light of all visible wavelengths strongly over a very short distance

evidence.citation: Vukusic P, Hallam B, Noyes J (2007). Brilliant whiteness in ultrathin beetle scales. Science 315: 348.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Synthetic scattering networks are lab-scale; cost and durability compared with titanium dioxide are unproven.

title: Morpho butterfly: structural colour without dyes
summary: The bright blue of Morpho butterflies comes from microscopic ridged structures on the wing scales that reflect blue light by interference, not from pigment. Structural colour can replace dyes and pigments in textiles, cosmetics, paints and security printing.
structure: ridges with stacked, tree-like lamellae of chitin and air
mechanism: multilayer interference reflects blue wavelengths, while slight irregularity between ridges spreads the colour over a wide viewing angle

evidence.citation: Vukusic P, Sambles JR, Lawrence CR, Wootton RJ (1999). Quantified interference and diffraction in single Morpho butterfly scales. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 266: 1403-1411.

Kinoshita S, Yoshioka S, Fujii Y, Okamoto N (2002). Mechanisms of structural colour in the Morpho butterfly: cooperation of regularity and irregularity in an iridescent scale. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 269: 1417-1421.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Structural colour depends on intact nanostructures; textile products have been costly and few reached market.

title: Pine cones: open and close with humidity, no motor
summary: Pine cone scales open when dry and close when wet, because two tissue layers swell differently with moisture. Architects copy the bilayer principle in facade panels and shading that adjust to weather without motors or electricity, cutting cooling energy in buildings.
structure: bilayer of tissues with different fibre orientation
mechanism: one layer swells much more with moisture than the other, so the scale bends like a bimetal strip as humidity changes

evidence.citation: Dawson C, Vincent JFV, Rocca AM (1997). How pine cones open. Nature 390: 668.

Reichert S, Menges A, Correa D (2015). Meteorosensitive architecture: biomimetic building skins based on materially embedded and hydraulically operated responsiveness. Computer-Aided Design 60: 50-69.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Responds to humidity, not to temperature or sunlight directly; wood-based facade elements need protection from decay and fatigue.

title: Holm oak: deep roots that keep trees green through summer drought
summary: Holm oaks in Mediterranean dehesas and woodlands survive long dry summers by reaching deep water with their roots and tightly controlling water loss. The trees stay green and keep giving shade and acorns when grass has dried, which is why they anchor the dehesa system.
structure: deep tap and sinker roots reaching groundwater
mechanism: access to deep water plus stomatal control keeps transpiration going through the dry season

evidence.citation: David TS, Henriques MO, Kurz-Besson C, et al. (2007). Water-use strategies in two co-occurring Mediterranean evergreen oaks: surviving the summer drought. Tree Physiology 27: 793-803.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Holm oaks under repeated extreme drought and root disease (Phytophthora) are declining in parts of Spain; resilience is not unlimited.

title: Mycorrhizal fungal networks between trees
summary: Most trees partner with soil fungi that trade water and nutrients for plant sugars, and one fungus can link several trees. This is a model of resource sharing for soil health and regenerative farming, but the popular 'wood wide web' story goes far beyond the evidence.
structure: fungal hyphae linking roots of neighbouring plants
mechanism: fungi exchange soil nutrients and water with plants for carbon; shared hyphae may move some resources between plants

evidence.citation: Simard SW, Perry DA, Jones MD, Myrold DD, Durall DM, Molina R (1997). Net transfer of carbon between ectomycorrhizal tree species in the field. Nature 388: 579-582.
Karst J, Jones MD, Hoeksema JD (2023). Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests. Nature Ecology & Evolution 7: 501-511.

popular_claim_note: Claims that 'mother trees' feed and warn their seedlings through a wood wide web are widely repeated. Karst et al. (2023) reviewed the field studies and found such claims are not supported by the evidence; the mycorrhizal partnership itself is well established.
caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Use for soil-health thinking, not as proof of tree-to-tree communication.

title: Cork from the cork oak: light, insulating, harvested without felling
summary: Cork is the bark of the cork oak, stripped by hand every nine years or so without cutting the tree. Its closed cells of gas make it light, insulating, springy and water-resistant. It is used for wine stoppers, thermal and acoustic insulation boards, flooring and light composite panels, and is grown in the Iberian montado and dehesa.
structure: closed, prism-shaped cells with thin suberin-rich walls

evidence.citation: Gibson LJ, Easterling KE, Ashby MF (1981). The structure and mechanics of cork. Proceedings of the Royal Society A 377: 99-117.
Silva SP, Sabino MA, Fernandes EM, Correlo VM, Boesel LF, Reis RL (2005). Cork: properties, capabilities and applications. International Materials Reviews 50: 345-365.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Supply is tied to slow-growing trees and a 9-year harvest cycle; agglomerates may contain synthetic binders that limit biodegradability.

title: Mycelium composites: packaging and panels grown from fungi and farm waste
summary: Fungal mycelium can be grown through crop residues such as hemp hurd or husks in a mould, binding them into a light foam-like part, then heat-treated to stop growth. The result is packaging and insulation panels that can be composted, an alternative to polystyrene foam.

evidence.citation: Jones M, Mautner A, Luenco S, Bismarck A, John S (2020). Engineered mycelium composite construction materials from fungal biorefineries: a critical review. Materials & Design 187: 108397.

Haneef M, Ceseracciu L, Canale C, Bayer IS, Heredia-Guerrero JA, Athanassiou A (2017). Advanced materials from fungal mycelium: fabrication and tuning of physical properties. Scientific Reports 7: 41292.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Mechanical strength is low and properties vary between batches; water uptake limits outdoor use. Compostability depends on any coatings added.

title: Natural-fibre and moulded-pulp packaging
summary: Moulded pulp made from recycled paper, bagasse or other plant fibres is formed into trays, egg boxes and protective inserts that are recyclable and compostable. Plant fibres such as hemp, jute and flax also replace plastics in bio-based packaging that biodegrades.

evidence.citation: Didone M, Saxena P, Brilhuis-Meijer E, Tosello G, Bissacco G, McAloone TC, Pigosso DCA, Howard TJ (2017). Moulded pulp manufacturing: overview and prospects for the process technology. Packaging Technology and Science 30: 231-249.
Faruk O, Bledzki AK, Fink HP, Sain M (2012). Biocomposites reinforced with natural fibers: 2000-2010. Progress in Polymer Science 37: 1552-1596.

known_products: moulded pulp egg cartons and trays
caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Barrier properties against water, grease and oxygen are weak without coatings; fluorinated grease-proofing coatings undo the environmental benefit.

title: Natural-fibre composites for lighter car interior parts
summary: Flax, hemp, kenaf and jute fibres in a polymer matrix are used for car door panels, parcel shelves and trim. They are lighter than glass-fibre parts, need less energy to produce and break more safely, helping make lighter structural and semi-structural components for cars.

evidence.citation: Holbery J, Houston D (2006). Natural-fiber-reinforced polymer composites in automotive applications. JOM 58: 80-86.
Faruk O, Bledzki AK, Fink HP, Sain M (2012). Biocomposites reinforced with natural fibers: 2000-2010. Progress in Polymer Science 37: 1552-1596.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Mostly used in non-structural or semi-structural interior parts; moisture sensitivity and variable fibre quality limit structural use, and most matrices are still fossil-based.

title: Chitosan from shellfish waste: films and coatings
summary: Chitosan is made from chitin in crab and shrimp shells left over from seafood processing. It forms films and edible coatings that slow spoilage of fruit and food, has antimicrobial activity and biodegrades, turning a waste stream into packaging and cosmetic ingredients.

evidence.citation: Rinaudo M (2006). Chitin and chitosan: properties and applications. Progress in Polymer Science 31: 603-632.
Elsabee MZ, Abdou ES (2013). Chitosan based edible films and coatings: a review. Materials Science and Engineering C 33: 1819-1841.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Making chitosan uses strong alkali and acid steps; films are sensitive to moisture, and shellfish allergy labelling may apply in food uses.

title: Seaweed alginate: gels and films for biodegradable packaging
summary: Alginate, extracted from brown seaweeds, forms gels and films when it meets calcium. It is used as a thickener and in wound dressings and is explored for edible and biodegradable packaging that replaces single-use plastic films and sachets.

evidence.citation: Lee KY, Mooney DJ (2012). Alginate: properties and biomedical applications. Progress in Polymer Science 37: 106-126.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The cited review covers alginate properties, mainly in medicine, not packaging performance; films are water-sensitive and seaweed harvesting must be managed sustainably.

title: PHA bioplastics made by bacteria
summary: Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) are polyesters that many bacteria store as energy reserves. Grown by fermentation on sugars, oils or waste streams, they can be moulded like conventional plastics and biodegrade in soil and sea water, making them a candidate for packaging that biodegrades.

evidence.citation: Chen GQ (2009). A microbial polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) based bio- and materials industry. Chemical Society Reviews 38: 2434-2446.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. PHA costs more than fossil plastics and biodegradation rates depend strongly on the environment. Developing new production strains would be genetic work needing legal review; this record covers the commercial material only.

title: Engineered timber: building with stored carbon
summary: Cross-laminated timber and glulam let wood replace concrete and steel in floors, walls and frames of mid-rise buildings. The wood stores carbon taken from the air, panels are made off-site, and timber from local, well-managed forests shortens supply chains.

evidence.citation: Ramage MH, Burridge H, Busse-Wicher M, et al. (2017). The wood from the trees: the use of timber in construction. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews 68: 333-359.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Carbon benefits depend on forest management and the building's end of life; fire, moisture and acoustic design need specialist engineering.

title: Hemp-lime (hempcrete) insulating walls
summary: Hemp-lime mixes the woody core of the hemp stalk with a lime binder to make non-load-bearing walls that insulate and buffer humidity. Hemp grows quickly on farmland and the lime reabsorbs some carbon dioxide as it sets.

evidence.citation: Shea A, Lawrence M, Walker P (2012). Hygrothermal performance of an experimental hemp-lime building. Construction and Building Materials 36: 270-275.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Low strength (needs a structural frame), slow drying, and performance results come from a small number of test buildings.

title: Biochar from farm and forestry residues
summary: Biochar is charcoal made by heating crop and wood residues with little oxygen. Added to soil it can store carbon for a long time and may improve water and nutrient retention, turning residues that would be burned or left to rot into a soil and carbon resource.

evidence.citation: Lehmann J, Gaunt J, Rondon M (2006). Bio-char sequestration in terrestrial ecosystems - a review. Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change 11: 403-427.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Crop-yield effects vary widely by soil and feedstock; carbon-credit claims need careful accounting of the pyrolysis process.

title: Biomineralisation: making hard materials at room temperature in water
summary: Shells, bones, teeth and sponge skeletons are built from minerals deposited at room temperature and normal pressure in water, guided by an organic template. Copying these process conditions points to ceramics and coatings made with far less energy than kilns and furnaces.

evidence.citation: Weiner S, Addadi L (1997). Design strategies in mineralized biological materials. Journal of Materials Chemistry 7: 689-702.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Describes the general principle only; work on a specific organism's mineralising proteins would be biochemical and need legal review. Industrial room-temperature ceramics remain largely at research stage.

title: Bacteria that lay down limestone: bio-cement and self-healing concrete
summary: Some soil bacteria precipitate calcium carbonate when fed urea or calcium salts. This is used to bind loose sand without cement and, with dormant spores mixed into concrete, to seal small cracks when water gets in. Because it relies on microbial biochemistry, the record waits for legal review before it can be served.

evidence.citation: DeJong JT, Fritzges MB, Nusslein K (2006). Microbially induced cementation to control sand response to undrained shear. Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering 132: 1381-1392.
Jonkers HM, Thijssen A, Muyzer G, Copuroglu O, Schlangen E (2010). Application of bacteria as self-healing agent for the development of sustainable concrete. Ecological Engineering 36: 230-235.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Quarantined: relies on microbial biochemistry, legal review pending. Urea-based routes release ammonium; crack healing works for narrow cracks only.

title: Growing bacterial cellulose sheets
summary: Certain bacteria spin pure cellulose nanofibres into a mat at the surface of a sugary culture. The mat is strong when dry and very absorbent, and is explored for packaging, textiles, wound dressings and cosmetics. Because it relies on microbial biochemistry, the record waits for legal review before it can be served.

evidence.citation: Iguchi M, Yamanaka S, Budhiono A (2000). Bacterial cellulose - a masterpiece of nature's arts. Journal of Materials Science 35: 261-270.
Klemm D, Heublein B, Fink HP, Bohn A (2005). Cellulose: fascinating biopolymer and sustainable raw material. Angewandte Chemie International Edition 44: 3358-3393.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Quarantined: relies on microbial biochemistry, legal review pending. Production is slow and costly compared with plant cellulose.

title: Anaerobic digestion: turning organic waste into biogas and fertiliser
summary: In closed tanks without oxygen, communities of microbes break down manure, food waste and sewage sludge into biogas (mainly methane) and a nutrient-rich digestate. This mirrors how ecosystems recycle dead matter and turns waste into energy and fertiliser.

evidence.citation: Mata-Alvarez J, Mace S, Llabres P (2000). Anaerobic digestion of organic solid wastes. An overview of research achievements and perspectives. Bioresource Technology 74: 3-16.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Methane leaks can cancel climate benefits; digestate needs management to avoid nutrient run-off.

title: Phytoremediation: plants that clean contaminated soil and water
summary: Some plants take up heavy metals or help microbes break down pollutants around their roots. Planting them on contaminated industrial land or in water can remove or stabilise pollution slowly and cheaply, while greening the site.

evidence.citation: Salt DE, Blaylock M, Kumar NPBA, Dushenkov V, Ensley BD, Chet I, Raskin I (1995). Phytoremediation: a novel strategy for the removal of toxic metals from the environment using plants. Nature Biotechnology 13: 468-474.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Slow (years to decades), limited to root depth, and contaminated plant material must be disposed of safely.

title: Biofilters: microbes that clean exhaust air and remove odours
summary: Air from factories, food plants or sewage works can be blown through a moist bed of compost, bark or other packing where microbes eat odorous and volatile organic compounds. It is a low-energy alternative to burning or chemical scrubbing for dilute pollutants.

evidence.citation: Mudliar S, Giri B, Padoley K, Satpute D, Dixit R, Bhatt P, Pandey R, Juwarkar A, Vaidya A (2010). Bioreactors for treatment of VOCs and odours - a review. Journal of Environmental Management 91: 1039-1054.

known_products: compost and bark biofilters at wastewater plants
caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Works for dilute, biodegradable pollutants only; beds need moisture control and periodic replacement.

title: Constructed wetlands: plants and microbes that treat wastewater
summary: Constructed wetlands copy natural marshes: wastewater flows slowly through gravel or soil planted with reeds, and plants and microbes remove organic matter, nutrients and some pathogens. They treat water with little energy and create habitat.

evidence.citation: Vymazal J (2011). Constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment: five decades of experience. Environmental Science & Technology 45: 61-69.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Need much more land than conventional plants and perform less well in cold climates; design depends on the wastewater type.

title: Aquaponics: fish waste feeds plants, plants clean water for fish
summary: Aquaponics links fish tanks to hydroponic beds: bacteria convert fish waste into nitrate that plants take up, and the cleaned water returns to the fish. One system's waste becomes another's input, as in an ecosystem.

evidence.citation: Goddek S, Delaide B, Mankasingh U, Ragnarsdottir KV, Jijakli H, Thorarinsdottir R (2015). Challenges of sustainable and commercial aquaponics. Sustainability 7: 4199-4224.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Commercial viability is limited so far; energy for pumps and heating can be significant.

title: Dehesa: oak wood-pasture combining trees, livestock and crops
summary: The dehesa of south-west Spain is a managed savanna of scattered holm and cork oaks over pasture, grazed by pigs, cattle and sheep, sometimes rotated with cereals. The trees give shade, acorns and cork; the livestock fertilise the soil. It is a working model of farmland that keeps biodiversity, soil and water while producing food and materials.

evidence.citation: Joffre R, Rambal S, Ratte JP (1999). The dehesa system of southern Spain and Portugal as a natural ecosystem mimic. Agroforestry Systems 45: 57-79.
Moreno G, Pulido FJ (2009). The functioning, management and persistence of dehesas. In: Rigueiro-Rodriguez A, McAdam J, Mosquera-Losada MR (eds) Agroforestry in Europe. Springer, 127-160.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Many dehesas lack tree regeneration because of overgrazing and oak decline; local management knowledge is not captured here and would need consent.

source_region.note: Agro-silvo-pastoral system of south-west Iberia; montado in Portugal.

title: Kalundborg industrial symbiosis: one plant's waste is another's input
summary: In Kalundborg, Denmark, a power station, refinery, pharmaceutical plant, plasterboard maker and the town exchange steam, water, gypsum and other by-products. Over decades these bilateral deals grew into a network like a food web, cutting resource use and waste.

evidence.citation: Ehrenfeld J, Gertler N (1997). Industrial ecology in practice: the evolution of interdependence at Kalundborg. Journal of Industrial Ecology 1: 67-79.
Chertow MR (2000). Industrial symbiosis: literature and taxonomy. Annual Review of Energy and the Environment 25: 313-337.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Kalundborg grew from local, trust-based deals over decades; planned eco-industrial parks copying it have often failed. Steel and metal plants are not part of Kalundborg itself.

title: Green roofs: cooling buildings, holding rainwater, adding habitat
summary: Planted roofs with a thin layer of growing medium shade and insulate the roof, cool it through evaporation, hold back rainwater and give insects and birds habitat. They reduce cooling energy for the top floors of buildings and stormwater peaks in cities.

evidence.citation: Oberndorfer E, Lundholm J, Bass B, et al. (2007). Green roofs as urban ecosystems: ecological structures, functions, and services. BioScience 57: 823-833.
Getter KL, Rowe DB (2006). The role of extensive green roofs in sustainable development. HortScience 41: 1276-1285.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Energy savings are largest for poorly insulated, low-rise buildings in hot climates; in dry summers irrigation may be needed, and the roof must carry the extra load.

title: Fog collection nets: capturing water from air in dry regions
summary: Fine mesh nets set up on coastal hills and mountains intercept fog and let droplets run into gutters and tanks. In places with frequent fog they capture water from air for villages, reforestation and farms without energy input.

evidence.citation: Klemm O, Schemenauer RS, Lummerich A, et al. (2012). Fog as a fresh-water resource: overview and perspectives. Ambio 41: 221-234.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Only practical where fog is frequent and predictable; projects have failed when maintenance and local ownership were missing.

title: Urban trees and green spaces: cooling streets and buildings
summary: Trees and parks cool cities by shading surfaces and through evaporation from leaves. Studies find green areas are on average cooler than surroundings, which can reduce cooling energy in nearby buildings and heat stress for people.

evidence.citation: Bowler DE, Buyung-Ali L, Knight TM, Pullin AS (2010). Urban greening to cool towns and cities: a systematic review of the empirical evidence. Landscape and Urban Planning 97: 147-155.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The review notes most studies are observational and the cooling effect on building energy is not directly measured; trees need water and space.

title: Flower strips and hedgerows for wild pollinators
summary: Sowing native flower strips and keeping hedgerows on farm and factory land feeds wild bees and other pollinators. Field studies link more wild pollinators to better fruit set in crops, even where honey bees are present.

evidence.citation: Garibaldi LA, Steffan-Dewenter I, Winfree R, et al. (2013). Wild pollinators enhance fruit set of crops regardless of honey bee abundance. Science 339: 1608-1611.
Blaauw BR, Isaacs R (2014). Flower plantings increase wild bee abundance and the pollination services provided to a pollination-dependent crop. Journal of Applied Ecology 51: 890-898.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Benefits take several seasons to appear and depend on native seed mixes and low pesticide use nearby.

title: Cover crops: keeping soil covered to build carbon and structure
summary: Growing cover crops between main crops keeps living roots in the soil, which adds organic matter, protects against erosion and feeds soil life. A meta-analysis found a consistent increase in soil carbon under cover crops.

evidence.citation: Poeplau C, Don A (2015). Carbon sequestration in agricultural soils via cultivation of cover crops - a meta-analysis. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment 200: 33-41.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Soil carbon gains level off over time and can be reversed; in dry Mediterranean systems cover crops compete with the main crop for water.

title: Rain gardens and sustainable drainage on industrial sites
summary: Rain gardens, swales, permeable paving and retention ponds let rainwater soak in and be cleaned by soil and plants instead of rushing into sewers. On factory and urban sites they cut flood peaks and pollution while adding green space.

evidence.citation: Fletcher TD, Shuster W, Hunt WF, et al. (2015). SUDS, LID, BMPs, WSUD and more - the evolution and application of terminology surrounding urban drainage. Urban Water Journal 12: 525-542.
Dietz ME (2007). Low impact development practices: a review of current research and recommendations for future directions. Water, Air, and Soil Pollution 186: 351-363.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Performance depends on soil infiltration and maintenance; contaminated industrial runoff may need pre-treatment.
